title: Hermann Weyl
wiki_lead:
Hermann Klaus Hugo Weyl ( VILE; German: [vaɪl]; 9 November 1885 – 8 December 1955) was a German mathematician, theoretical physicist, logician and philosopher. He was one of the most influential mathematicians of the twentieth century. Although much of his working life was spent in Zürich, Switzerland, and then Princeton, New Jersey, he is associated with the University of Göttingen tradition of mathematics, represented by Carl Friedrich Gauss, David Hilbert and Hermann Minkowski.
Weyl made significant contributions to an exceptionally wide range of intellectual fields, including mathematics, physics, philosophy and logic, with interests extending to the nature of space, time, matter and symmetry, as well as the history of mathematics. The originator of gauge theory, which became a fundamental framework of particle physics, Weyl was a pioneer in applying group theory to quantum mechanics, and made foundational contributions to many branches of mathematics such as differential geometry and number theory. He developed or introduced concepts and results such as gauge invariance, the Peter–Weyl theorem, equidistribution theorem and the Weyl law. 
He was one of the first to conceive of combining general relativity with the laws of electromagnetism. In cosmology, he theoretically derived the linear redshift–distance relation later known as Hubble's redshift law, several years before Hubble's observations. 
An important member of the Institute for Advanced Study during its early years, Weyl conceived of mathematics as an organic whole, a view informed by his philosophical outlook, and this conception shaped his work across disciplines. Freeman Dyson wrote that Weyl alone bore comparison with the "last great universal mathematicians of the nineteenth century", Henri Poincaré and David Hilbert. Vladimir Arnold and Aleksei Parshin said that his mathematical, philosophical, physical and literary breadth made him “a phenomenon of twentieth-century German culture in entirety".

Hermann Klaus Hugo Weyl ( VILE; German: [vaɪl]; 9 November 1885 – 8 December 1955) was a German mathematician, theoretical physicist, logician and philosopher. He was one of the most influential mathematicians of the twentieth century. Although much of his working life was spent in Zürich, Switzerland, and then Princeton, New Jersey, he is associated with the University of Göttingen tradition of mathematics, represented by Carl Friedrich Gauss, David Hilbert and Hermann Minkowski.
Weyl made significant contributions to an exceptionally wide range of intellectual fields, including mathematics, physics, philosophy and logic, with interests extending to the nature of space, time, matter and symmetry, as well as the history of mathematics. The originator of gauge theory, which became a fundamental framework of particle physics, Weyl was a pioneer in applying group theory to quantum mechanics, and made foundational contributions to many branches of mathematics such as differential geometry and number theory. He developed or introduced concepts and results such as gauge invariance, the Peter–Weyl theorem, equidistribution theorem and the Weyl law. 
He was one of the first to conceive of combining general relativity with the laws of electromagnetism. In cosmology, he theoretically derived the linear redshift–distance relation later known as Hubble's redshift law, several years before Hubble's observations. 
An important member of the Institute for Advanced Study during its early years, Weyl conceived of mathematics as an organic whole, a view informed by his philosophical outlook, and this conception shaped his work across disciplines. Freeman Dyson wrote that Weyl alone bore comparison with the "last great universal mathematicians of the nineteenth century", Henri Poincaré and David Hilbert. Vladimir Arnold and Aleksei Parshin said that his mathematical, philosophical, physical and literary breadth made him “a phenomenon of twentieth-century German culture in entirety".


Biography
Hermann Weyl was born in Elmshorn, a small town near Hamburg, in Germany, and attended the Gymnasium Christianeum in Altona. His father, Ludwig Weyl, was a banker; whereas his mother, Anna Weyl (née Dieck), came from a wealthy family.
From 1904 to 1908, he studied mathematics and physics at both the University of Göttingen and the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. His doctorate was awarded at the University of Göttingen under the supervision of David Hilbert, whom he greatly admired.
In 1913, Weyl married Friederike Bertha Helene Joseph, known as Helene or Hella.

Helene had studied philosophy and mathematics at the University of Göttingen, where she attended the lectures of phenomenologist Edmund Husserl. She later became a translator of Spanish and English literature into German, particularly the works of Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset. Helene's studies under Husserl seem to have helped stimulate Weyl's interest in phenomenology, although Weyl had himself attended Husserl's lectures during his student years in Göttingen. Weyl and Helene had two sons, Fritz Joachim Weyl and Michael Weyl, both of whom were born in Zürich, Switzerland. Helene died in Princeton, New Jersey, on 5 September 1948. A memorial service in her honor was held in Princeton on 9 September 1948. Speakers at her memorial service included her son Fritz Joachim Weyl and mathematicians Oswald Veblen and Richard Courant. In 1950, Weyl married sculptor Ellen Bär (née Lohnstein), who was the widow of professor Richard Josef Bär of Zürich.
After taking a teaching post for a few years, Weyl left Göttingen in 1913 for Zurich to take the chair of mathematics. There he overlapped with Albert Einstein, who, together with Marcel Grossmann, was working on the mathematical formulation of general relativity. Einstein's work helped ignite Weyl's interest in mathematical physics, particularly the theory of relativity. In 1921, Weyl met Erwin Schrödinger, a theoretical physicist who at the time was a professor at the University of Zurich. They were to become close friends over time. Weyl and Schrödinger's wife, Annemarie ("Anny") Schrödinger, began a relationship that lasted for several years that Schrödinger learned of only in the early 1930s. By that time the Schrödingers were living in an open marriage, and the revelation did not damage his friendship with Weyl.
Weyl was a Plenary Speaker of the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in 1928 at Bologna and an Invited Speaker of the ICM in 1936 at Oslo. For the academic year 1928–1929, he was a visiting professor at Princeton University where he wrote a paper, "On a problem in the theory of groups arising in the foundations of infinitesimal geometry," with Howard P. Robertson.
In 1930, Weyl left the University of Zürich to succeed David Hilbert as professor of mathematics at the University of Göttingen. He remained there until 1933, when he left Germany in opposition to the Nazi regime. His decision was also influenced by the fact that his wife, Helene, was Jewish and their sons were classified as Jewish under Nazi racial laws. Abraham Flexner, the director of the newly established Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, had first approached Weyl about joining its faculty in 1932. Although Weyl initially accepted the offer,  he later declined it after the death of his mother-in-law and an outbreak of influenza in his household. As conditions in Germany deteriorated, Flexner renewed the offer in September 1933, and Weyl accepted. He joined the Institute's faculty that year and remained there until his retirement in 1951, when he became Professor Emeritus. After retiring, he divided his time between Princeton and Zürich with his second wife Ellen Bär. He died of a heart attack in Zürich on 8 December 1955.
Weyl was cremated in Zurich on 12 December 1955. His remains were subsequently interred in a columbarium at Princeton Cemetery in 1999.
The remains of Weyl's son Michael Weyl (1917–2011) are interred right next to Hermann's ashes in the same columbarium vault.
Weyl's conception of God has been recognised as similar to the philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, particularly his understanding of God or nature.


Working Style
According to Max Newman, Weyl’s working style was characterised by a conceptual theme: he preferred arguments emerging from the central core of a problem to computational verification, and often favoured verbal formulations over symbolic ones. Nevertheless, this taste for general theories did not diminish his rigour for mathematical detail, and he regarded examples as essential to mathematical understanding. Newman described his writing as leisurely and rich in ideas. Schrödinger was astonished about how he found Weyl’s written explanations harder to follow than his speech. He attributed this to mathematical objects and conclusions being so apparent to Weyl that he sometimes omitted intermediate steps other people considered necessary. Schrödinger attributed this partly to Weyl’s aesthetic sensibility.


Mathematics

Hermann Weyl's work had a foundational influence on much of mathematics. In particular, he is credited with deeply shaping several fields, including differential geometry, topological groups, Lie groups, representation theory, harmonic analysis, analytic number theory and spectral theory. Claude Chevalley and André Weil credited Weyl's work with contributing greatly to the shift in mathematical thinking from the classical conception of mathematics, founded on the real number, to the modern conception, founded on the notion of structure.
Max Newman wrote that Weyl was at the peak of his powers between 1917 and 1927, adding: "A stream of papers appeared, not only on his main themes, but on any mathematical topics that interested him—and that meant in almost all parts of mathematics."


Manifolds and Topology
Weyl's 1913 book, Die Idee der Riemannschen Fläche (The Concept of a Riemann Surface), based on his Göttingen lectures of 1911–12, provided the first precise axiomatic definition of an abstract manifold.
 At the time, the theory of Riemann surfaces, pioneered by Bernhard Riemann and Felix Klein, was not a fully rigorous field and relied on intuitive geometry in large part. Weyl's work grounded this more intuitive picture with a systematic foundation. He defined the concept of a two-dimensional topological manifold abstractly by using a list of axioms which are independent of any embedding in a larger space. Holomorphic transition functions were then added between coordinate charts, creating a complex-analytic manifold, a Riemann surface in the modern sense. The work laid the axiomatic foundations for the theory of Riemann surfaces, by becoming the model for all subsequent kinds of manifolds studied in the twentieth century, such as differentiable, complex, Riemannian, and symplectic manifolds. The book also gave a new proof of the Dirichlet principle, following Hilbert, to establish the existence of global meromorphic functions on these surfaces.  Mathematician Leo Sario described Weyl's 1913 publication as "undoubtedly [having] a greater influence on the development of geometric function theory than any other publication since Riemann's dissertation." 


Differential Geometry
By 1915, Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity had successfully described gravity as the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime. However, electromagnetism remained a separate force, described by Maxwell's equations rather than by geometry. It was widely felt that a truly fundamental theory should not treat these as two unrelated phenomena, but should show some sort of unity; Einstein himself considered it a primary shortcoming of his theory that it did not unify gravitation and electromagnetism.
Weyl found it philosophically and mathematically unsatisfying that Riemannian geometry allowed for the direct comparison of lengths at distant points, which he saw as a "last element of geometry 'at a distance'" and an accidental remnant of its Euclidean origins. He argued that a "true infinitesimal geometry" should only permit the comparison of lengths at the same point or at infinitesimally close points. His ambition was to construct a geometry based on this purely infinitesimal principle. His insight was that in the process of fixing this perceived mathematical flaw, the resulting geometric structure would also naturally accommodate the electromagnetic field.
In 1918, Weyl introduced a generalisation of Riemannian geometry known as Weyl geometry, based on a local scale (gauge) symmetry. In it, the length of a vector is not constant when it is moved from one point to another, so its length can change depending on the path taken. This change is described by a new field, a 1-form Aμ, which mathematically acts as the electromagnetic four-potential. The gravitational field is described by the spacetime metric (as in general relativity), while the electromagnetic field is described by the new gauge field Aμ that dictates how lengths change from point to point. Both are now facets of a single, unified geometric structure. From this framework Weyl derived a tensor that exists as a Riemannian conformal object, not something that subsists only within Weyl’s full gauge geometry. This tensor, later called the Weyl tensor, is the trace-free part of the Riemann curvature tensor and is conformally invariant. The Weyl tensor became a fundamental object in differential geometry and general relativity, where it describes tidal forces and gravitational waves.
Einstein critiqued the physical aspect of Weyl’s theory, noting that if the length of a vector is path-dependent, then the rate of a clock (whose ticking is based on a physical length, such as the size of an atom) would also depend on its history.
